`InOutBuf<'inp, 'out, T>`: the same in-place-or-disjoint buffer pair, in production cryptographic Rust, with a safe API over raw pointers.
The fully safe `Option<Box<Node<T>>>` list of *Learning Rust With Entirely Too Many Linked Lists*.

The safe `Option<Box<Node<T>>>` list: `push`, `pop`, `peek`, and its iterators.

`std`'s ring buffer, with the same head/len circular layout, over an `unsafe` `RawVec`.
A bit set over a `Vec` of words, in safe Rust, with the same word-index/bit-offset arithmetic and word-wise `|`.
`std::collections::LinkedList`: the same doubly-linked list, with `Option<NonNull<Node<T>>>` links and `unsafe` throughout.
A small, self-contained free list of exactly this shape: `*mut usize` links written into the freed blocks themselves.
A four-level x86-64 page-table walker in Rust: the same walk/map/unmap operations, `unsafe` because the frames are physical memory.
`std`'s vector: `len`/`capacity`, the initialized prefix, and `push` on a full buffer.

countingRules.uncountedAttribute: a Rust attribute with no verification content (`#[inline]`, `#[derive(…)]`, `#[stable(…)]`) is metadata, and is not counted
countingRules.spec: specifications and annotations: pre/postconditions, invariants, representation predicates, theorem statements, ghost state, attributes
countingRules.relevantLine: at least 4 characters after comment removal, not delimiters only, not import/module/scope boilerplate
countingRules.proof: proof material: tactic scripts, proof blocks, asserts, ghost steps
countingRules.code: computational content executed at run time

safeRust.reason: The links are intrusive: `prev`/`next` live in a frame's own metadata slot and point at frames the list does not own, so a node is reachable both from the list and from whoever holds the frame. Safe Rust cannot express that sharing; the safe encoding replaces the links by indices into an arena, and loses the O(1) unlink of a frame one already holds.

coverage.note: The source is the whole `LinkedList` API — `push_back`, `pop_back`, `size`, `contains`, three cursor constructors, iterators; the port answers `push_front`, `pop_front` and `CursorMut::take_current`.

safeRust.reason: The tree is safe Rust (`Option<Box<Node>>`), but the paper's iterative leftmost-leaf traversal keeps a `&mut` derived inside a loop — NLL problem case #3 — which today's borrow checker rejects and which Polonius is meant to accept. The safe workarounds are recursion or an index path.

safeRust.reason: The type is a pair of raw pointers whose safety condition is exactly `src == dst` or `src` and `dst` disjoint, and its `unsafe` constructor asks the caller for it. Safe Rust can encode the two shapes as an enum — `&mut [T]` in place, `(&[T], &mut [T])` disjoint — but the aliasing choice then becomes a run-time tag matched at every call site, instead of the ghost state this file makes it.

safeRust.reason: Every node is pointed at by its predecessor's `next` and its successor's `prev`, so ownership cannot be a tree. Safe Rust needs either `Rc<RefCell<…>>`, paying run-time borrow checks and leaking the cycle, or an arena of indices; `std` chooses raw pointers behind a safe API.

coverage.note: The whole example, list and iterator alike; only the `main` that demonstrates it is left out.

safeRust.reason: A free list threads its links through memory that is by definition owned by nothing: the block being freed is raw bytes, and its first word is reinterpreted as a `Node`. That is the archetypal use of `unsafe`.

safeRust.reason: The tables are physical frames reached through raw addresses in a hardware-defined layout, and the executable side reads and writes entries in memory the type system does not own. The recursive `PTTreeNode` model above it is pure, and would be safe Rust.

safeRust.reason: This module has no program: it is the ghost permission layer Verus needs because the code it verifies uses raw pointers. Safe Rust needs no such layer — a `Vec<T>` and an index give the same reasoning for free — which is exactly why it is kept separate here.

comparisons.note: The `vstd` layer a Verus development gets for free: sequences plus the manipulation of `PointsTo` permissions. Counted so that a Lean-versus-Verus comparison is not charged twice for the same library.
